tool.name: Zsh
tool.tagline: Interactive shell with powerful completion, globbing and customization
tool.description: Zsh is a Bourne-style Unix shell, largely compatible with bash, that adds a programmable completion system, rich globbing, a highly configurable line editor and prompt, and a large plugin ecosystem. It has been the default shell on macOS since Catalina, and many developers on Linux adopt it for a faster, friendlier terminal. Learning it well means fewer keystrokes every day and a shell configuration you understand rather than copy-paste.

glossary.def: A shell you type commands into. Scripts run in non-interactive shells, which skip things only people need, like the prompt and aliases.
Zsh's completion system: it knows the options and arguments of many commands and completes them when you press Tab. compinit switches it on.
The zsh command that sets styles: named settings, mainly for completion, that apply wherever a context pattern matches, e.g. zstyle ':completion:*' menu select.
Zsh's list of directories to search for function and completion files, also available as the variable $fpath.
Using ** in a file pattern to match through any number of directories, e.g. **/*.py for every Python file below the current directory.
In zsh, a filter in parentheses at the end of a file pattern, e.g. *(.) for ordinary files only or *(om[1]) for the newest file.
In zsh, a colon code that changes a file name or variable: :t keeps the file name, :h the directory part, :r drops the ending, :e keeps only the ending.
A % code in a zsh prompt that is replaced when the prompt is drawn, e.g. %~ (current directory) or %? (last exit status).
A zsh alias made with alias -g that is replaced anywhere on the line, not only in the first word, e.g. G for | grep.
A zsh alias made with alias -s that opens files by their ending: after alias -s md=less, typing README.md runs less README.md.
A popular zsh framework: a ready-made bundle of settings, hundreds of plugins and prompt themes, switched on from ~/.zshrc.
The Zsh Line Editor: the part of zsh that handles what you type at the prompt, made of widgets you can bind to keys.
In zsh, one editing action of the line editor, such as moving the cursor or searching history; you can bind widgets to keys and write your own.
A table that connects key presses to actions; in zsh, bindkey edits it, e.g. emacs-style or vi-style keys.
In zsh, letters in parentheses inside ${...} that change the value, e.g. ${(U)name} for upper case or ${(s:,:)csv} to split at commas.
Zsh's way to declare a function whose body is read from a file on fpath only the first time it is called.

concepts.name: Zsh vs bash, and switching
concepts.summary: What zsh adds over bash, how to check which shell you're in, and how to make zsh the shell you get when you log in.
concepts.why: You need to know which shell is reading your commands before any configuration makes sense.
concepts.body:
Zsh (the Z shell) is another shell, a close relative of bash: everyday commands, pipes, redirections, variables, `if` and `for` work the same way. What it adds is mostly for typing at the **prompt**, the short text a shell shows when it's waiting for your command:

- smarter completion when you press Tab, knowing the options of hundreds of commands,
- file patterns that search every folder below the current one, with filters,
- spelling correction, and history shared between terminal windows,
- a prompt and line editing you can program,
- many **plugins**: add-on scripts, written by other people, that you can switch on.

It has been the standard shell on **macOS since 10.15 Catalina**; on Linux you install it like any other software (`sudo apt install zsh` on Ubuntu).

When you log in, or open a terminal on a Mac, the system starts your **login shell**: the shell recorded for your account. `$SHELL` holds that recorded shell, which isn't necessarily the one you're running right now; `ps -p $$` or `echo $ZSH_VERSION` tells you the current one.

Change your login shell with `chsh -s "$(command -v zsh)"`, where `$(command -v zsh)` is replaced by the location of the zsh program, such as `/bin/zsh`. That location must be listed in `/etc/shells`, and the change applies the next time you log in.

Like bash, zsh runs **startup files** when it starts: files holding your settings, mainly `~/.zshrc` (next lesson). The first time zsh starts without one, it offers a setup menu (`zsh-newuser-install`); you can quit it and write the file yourself. `zsh -f` starts a shell that skips all startup files, handy for testing whether a problem comes from your settings.

Switching the shell you type in doesn't change scripts: a script starting with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` still runs in bash. Keep writing scripts that must run everywhere in bash, and enjoy zsh in your terminal.

One word to know: Unix people call folders **directories**, and zsh's messages and these lessons do too.
concepts.code:
zsh --version                 # zsh 5.9 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu)
echo $SHELL                   # your login shell, e.g. /bin/zsh
ps -p $$ -o comm=             # the shell you are actually in: zsh
echo $ZSH_VERSION             # 5.9  (empty in bash)
grep zsh /etc/shells          # /bin/zsh /usr/bin/zsh  (allowed for chsh)
chsh -s "$(command -v zsh)"   # make zsh your login shell; log in again
zsh -f                        # a clean zsh that skips your settings files
./deploy.sh                   # a #!/usr/bin/env bash script still runs in bash
takeaways: Zsh works like bash for everyday commands and adds features for typing at the prompt
$SHELL is the login shell; ps -p $$ shows the current shell
chsh -s changes the login shell; scripts follow their shebang
pitfalls: Assuming $SHELL tells you which shell is running right now.

quiz.q: You switched your terminal to zsh. Which shell runs a script whose first line is #!/usr/bin/env bash?
quiz.explain: The shebang line decides which program runs the script, whatever shell you type in.

quiz.q: What is `zsh -f` useful for?
options: Running zsh faster by skipping completion only
Starting zsh without any startup files to test your settings
quiz.explain: -f skips the startup files, so you can tell whether a problem comes from your settings.

concepts.name: Startup files: .zshenv, .zprofile, .zshrc
concepts.summary: Which zsh settings file is read when, and what belongs in each one.
concepts.why: Putting settings in the wrong file causes slow scripts, missing PATH entries and confusing behaviour.
concepts.body:
Zsh reads up to four startup files from your home directory, each right after a system-wide version in `/etc`. Which ones depends on the kind of shell. An **interactive shell** is one you type into; a script runs in a non-interactive one. A login shell is the first one started when you log in.

- `~/.zshenv`: read by **every** zsh, including scripts and `zsh -c 'command'`. Keep it tiny and silent: a few environment variables at most.
- `~/.zprofile`: login shells, before `.zshrc`. A good place for `PATH` and other environment variables.
- `~/.zshrc`: **interactive** shells. Aliases, options, completion, keyboard shortcuts and the prompt go here.
- `~/.zlogin`: login shells, after `.zshrc`; rarely needed. `~/.zlogout` runs when a login shell exits.

Unlike bash, an interactive login shell reads **both** `.zprofile` and `.zshrc`, so there's no need to load one from the other. On macOS every new Terminal tab is a login shell, while most Linux terminal programs start non-login shells.

On macOS, `/etc/zprofile` runs a tool called `path_helper` that reorders `PATH`, so directories you add in `.zshenv` can end up behind the system's own. That's another reason to set `PATH` in `.zprofile`.

`ZDOTDIR` moves these files somewhere else (for example to `~/.config/zsh`); set it in `~/.zshenv`. After editing, `exec zsh` replaces your current shell with a fresh one. That's cleaner than `source ~/.zshrc`, because settings you deleted from the file really disappear.
concepts.code:
# Order for an interactive login shell (e.g. a macOS Terminal tab):
#   /etc/zshenv  ~/.zshenv  ->  /etc/zprofile  ~/.zprofile
#   ->  /etc/zshrc  ~/.zshrc  ->  /etc/zlogin  ~/.zlogin
# ~/.zshenv   : every zsh, scripts included -> keep it tiny
export EDITOR=vim
# ~/.zprofile : login shells -> PATH and environment variables
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
# ~/.zshrc    : interactive shells -> aliases, options, prompt, completion
alias ll='ls -lah'
setopt AUTO_CD                # type a directory's name alone to go into it
# Reload after editing:
exec zsh
# See which files actually run at startup:
zsh -o SOURCE_TRACE -i -c exit 2>&1 | head
takeaways: .zshenv: every shell, keep it minimal; .zprofile: login; .zshrc: interactive
Interactive login shells read both .zprofile and .zshrc
`exec zsh` reloads cleanly
pitfalls: Printing output or running slow commands in ~/.zshenv, which then affects every script and every remote file copy with scp.

quiz.q: Where should aliases and the prompt be defined?
quiz.explain: .zshrc is read by interactive shells, the only ones that use aliases and a prompt.

quiz.q: Which file is read even by a non-interactive `zsh script.zsh`?
quiz.explain: .zshenv is read by every zsh, unless it's started with -f.

concepts.name: Tab completion
concepts.summary: Turn on zsh's completion system, get a menu you can move through, and complete options, branch names, machine names and paths.
concepts.why: Completion is zsh's single biggest time-saver, and it takes two lines to switch on.
concepts.body:
**Tab completion** means the shell finishes what you're typing when you press Tab: the rest of a file name, a command, an option. Bash does some of it; zsh's completion system, **compsys**, knows the options and arguments of hundreds of commands. You switch it on by loading and running a command called `compinit`; ready-made setups such as **Oh My Zsh**, a popular bundle of zsh settings and add-ons (see the plugins lesson), do this for you. Once it's on:

- `git checkout <Tab>` offers your branch names, `ssh <Tab>` the machines in your ssh settings file, `kill <Tab>` running programs, and `tar -<Tab>` options with descriptions,
- shortened paths expand: `cd /u/lo/b<Tab>` becomes `cd /usr/local/bin/`,
- pressing Tab again cycles through the choices, and Ctrl-D lists them without inserting one.

Settings for completion are made with **zstyle**, which sets a style (a setting) together with a pattern saying where it applies. The two most popular: `zstyle ':completion:*' menu select` gives a menu you move through with the arrow keys, and a `matcher-list` style makes matching ignore upper and lower case. Styles are covered in depth in the Expert lesson on writing completions.

`compinit` saves what it finds in a **cache** file, `~/.zcompdump`, so the next start is quicker. If a newly installed tool has no completion, delete that file and start a new shell. compinit also checks that nobody else can change the directories it loads completions from, and warns about "insecure directories" otherwise; `compaudit` lists them so you can fix their permissions instead of silencing the check.

Zsh finds completion files through **fpath**, a list of directories (plugins add theirs to it). Run `compinit` after anything that changes `fpath`, otherwise those completions aren't found.
concepts.code:
# ~/.zshrc
autoload -Uz compinit && compinit        # turn on the completion system
zstyle ':completion:*' menu select       # arrow-key menu of choices
zstyle ':completion:*' matcher-list 'm:{a-z}={A-Za-z}'   # ignore upper/lower case
zstyle ':completion:*:descriptions' format '%B%d%b'      # bold group headings
# Then try, pressing Tab where marked:
#   cd /u/lo/b<Tab>      ->  cd /usr/local/bin/
#   git checkout ma<Tab> ->  matching branch names
#   tar -<Tab>           ->  every option with a description
#   kill <Tab>           ->  running programs with their ID numbers
#   ssh <Tab>            ->  servers from ~/.ssh/config and known_hosts
compaudit                                # lists insecure completion directories, if any
rm -f ~/.zcompdump && exec zsh           # rebuild the completion cache
takeaways: `autoload -Uz compinit && compinit` switches completion on
zstyle ':completion:*' menu select gives a menu you can move through
Delete ~/.zcompdump when new completions don't show up
pitfalls: Running compinit before plugins add their directories to fpath, so their completions are missing.

quiz.q: What does `zstyle ':completion:*' menu select` change?
options: Completion is switched off for menus
Choices can be picked with the arrow keys
Completion starts ignoring upper and lower case
quiz.explain: menu select turns the list of choices into a menu you move through.

quiz.q: A tool you just installed has a completion file but Tab does nothing. A likely fix?
options: Delete ~/.zcompdump and start a new shell
quiz.explain: compinit caches the completions it found in ~/.zcompdump; rebuilding it picks up new ones.

concepts.name: Recursive globs and qualifiers
concepts.summary: Use ** to match files in every directory below, and glob qualifiers like (.), (/) and (om) to filter and sort the matches.
concepts.why: Zsh patterns replace many longer commands with something short you can type at the prompt.
concepts.body:
Zsh understands the same `*`, `?` and `[...]` patterns as bash (also called **globs**), plus a few extras that make it shine at the prompt.

**Recursive globbing** is always on: `**/` matches any number of directories, so `**/*.py` matches Python files here and in every directory below, however deep. Bash needs `shopt -s globstar` for this.

**Glob qualifiers** go in parentheses at the end of a pattern and filter or sort the matches:

- `(.)` ordinary files, `(/)` directories, `(@)` **symbolic links** (shortcuts that point to another file), `(*)` files you can run,
- `(om)` sort by when the file was last changed, newest first; `(on)` by name,
- `[1]` or `[1,3]` take the first match or a range: `*(om[1])` is the newest file,
- `(N)` makes this pattern turn into nothing if it matches nothing.

The biggest difference from bash: when a pattern matches nothing, zsh reports **"no matches found"** and doesn't run the command at all (the `NOMATCH` option). Bash would pass the pattern along unchanged. This bites with internet links and other arguments that contain `?`, `*` or `[`, such as `curl https://x.io/?q=1` (curl downloads from the internet) or `pip install foo[dev]`. Put them in quotes, or start the command with `noglob`.

Use `print -l` (one item per line) to preview what a pattern turns into before you use it with `rm` or `mv`.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"              # a fresh temporary directory
mkdir -p src/lib && touch src/a.py src/lib/b.py notes.txt
print -l **/*.py        # src/a.py  src/lib/b.py   (every directory below)
print -l *(/)           # src         (directories only)
print -l **/*(.)        # every ordinary file, in every directory below
touch -d '2 days ago' old.txt
print -l *.txt(om)      # notes.txt old.txt   (newest first)
print -l *.txt(om[1])   # notes.txt           (just the newest)
print -l *.zip(N)       # (nothing: N = empty if no match)
print 'https://x.io/?q=1'   # quote web addresses: ? is a pattern character
ls *.zip                # zsh: no matches found: *.zip
takeaways: ** reaches every directory below, always on
Qualifiers like (.) (/) (om[1]) filter and sort matches
No match is an error in zsh; quote links or use (N) / noglob
pitfalls: Running `pip install requests[socks]` (a Python install command) unquoted and getting 'no matches found'.

quiz.q: Which glob expands to the most recently modified file in the directory?
quiz.explain: om sorts by last change, newest first, and [1] picks the first match.

quiz.q: `curl https://api.example.com/items?id=4` fails with 'no matches found'. Why?
options: The ? is treated as a pattern that matches no file
quiz.explain: An unquoted ? is a pattern character; zsh refuses to run a command whose pattern matches nothing.

concepts.name: Options and shared history
concepts.summary: Turn zsh behaviour on and off with setopt, and configure a large, shared, de-duplicated history.
concepts.why: A handful of options and history settings make the shell noticeably nicer to live in.
concepts.body:
Most zsh behaviour is controlled by named **options**. `setopt NAME` turns one on, `unsetopt NAME` (or `setopt NO_NAME`) turns it off. Names ignore upper and lower case and underscores, so `AUTO_CD`, `autocd` and `AutoCd` are the same option. Plain `setopt` lists the options that differ from their defaults, and `[[ -o name ]]` tests one.

Popular options for typing at the prompt:

- `AUTO_CD`: type a directory's name alone to go into it,
- `AUTO_PUSHD` and `PUSHD_IGNORE_DUPS`: every cd also remembers the directory on a stack (a pile where the latest is on top); `cd -<Tab>` and `dirs -v` let you jump back,
- `INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS`: allow `#` comments at the prompt (off by default!),
- `CORRECT`: offer to fix mistyped commands.

**History** isn't saved unless you set it up. Set `HISTFILE` to a file name, `HISTSIZE` (how many entries the shell keeps while it runs) and `SAVEHIST` (how many it writes to the file). Then add:

- `SHARE_HISTORY`: all open shells read and add to the same history as you go,
- `HIST_IGNORE_ALL_DUPS`: drop older duplicates,
- `HIST_IGNORE_SPACE`: commands typed with a space in front aren't recorded, handy for ones that contain a password,
- `EXTENDED_HISTORY`: also record when each command ran and how long it took.

`history` (short for `fc -l`) shows entries and `history -i` adds dates and times. `!!` (the previous command), `!$` (its last argument) and `!git` (the last command starting with git) work as in bash.
concepts.code:
# ~/.zshrc
setopt AUTO_CD                        # 'projects' alone -> cd projects
setopt AUTO_PUSHD PUSHD_IGNORE_DUPS   # cd builds a stack: cd -<Tab>, dirs -v
setopt INTERACTIVE_COMMENTS           # allow # comments at the prompt
setopt CORRECT                        # zsh: correct 'gti' to 'git' [nyae]?
HISTFILE=~/.zsh_history
HISTSIZE=50000                        # entries kept in memory
SAVEHIST=50000                        # entries written to HISTFILE
setopt SHARE_HISTORY                  # all shells share one live history
setopt HIST_IGNORE_ALL_DUPS HIST_IGNORE_SPACE EXTENDED_HISTORY
# At the prompt:
setopt                                # options that differ from defaults
[[ -o autocd ]] && echo "autocd on"   # case and underscores do not matter
history -i -5                         # last 5 entries with timestamps
takeaways: setopt / unsetopt; names ignore case and underscores
History is only saved with HISTFILE and SAVEHIST set
SHARE_HISTORY and HIST_IGNORE_SPACE are favourite history options
pitfalls: Expecting history to be saved without setting HISTFILE and SAVEHIST.

quiz.q: Which pair of settings is needed for zsh to write history to disk?
quiz.explain: HISTFILE names the file and SAVEHIST says how many entries to write to it.

quiz.q: Are `setopt AUTO_CD` and `setopt autocd` the same?
options: Yes: option names ignore case and underscores
No, only the upper-case form works
No, autocd is a different option
quiz.explain: Zsh treats option names the same whatever their case and underscores.

concepts.name: Customizing the prompt
concepts.summary: Build a prompt with % codes, colours, a success-or-failure marker and the git branch via vcs_info.
concepts.why: A good prompt shows where you are, which branch you are on and whether the last command failed.
concepts.body:
The prompt is the `PROMPT` variable (also called `PS1`); `RPROMPT` is shown on the right and gets out of the way as you type into it. Zsh replaces **percent escapes** in them:

- `%n` your user name, `%m` the machine's short name, `%~` the directory you're in, with `~` for home, `%1~` only its last part,
- `%#` shows `#` for root (the administrator) and `%` otherwise, `%?` the last exit status, `%T` the time,
- `%F{red}...%f` text colour (names or 0-255), `%B...%b` bold,
- `%(?.yes.no)` a choice: shows "yes" if the last command succeeded, "no" otherwise.

To show values that change, such as variables or the output of **functions** (named groups of commands you define, like `greet() { echo hi; }`), set `PROMPT_SUBST` and write the prompt in **single quotes**. Then `${...}` is filled in each time the prompt is drawn, rather than once when `.zshrc` runs.

For the branch of a git project, zsh ships **vcs_info**: load it, call `vcs_info` from `precmd` (a function zsh runs by itself before drawing each prompt), and use `$vcs_info_msg_0_`. Its `formats` style uses `%b` for the branch; it can also show changes you haven't committed.

`print -P '...'` fills in prompt escapes so you can experiment. If you prefer a ready-made prompt, Powerlevel10k and Starship (which works in several shells) are popular, but knowing the escapes lets you read and tweak them.
concepts.code:
autoload -Uz vcs_info
precmd() { vcs_info }                       # refresh before each prompt
zstyle ':vcs_info:git:*' formats ' (%b)'    # %b = branch name
setopt PROMPT_SUBST
PROMPT='%F{cyan}%n@%m%f %F{yellow}%~%f${vcs_info_msg_0_} %(?.%F{green}.%F{red})%#%f '
RPROMPT='%F{240}%T%f'                       # time on the right
print -P '%F{yellow}%~%f'                   # try escapes: ~/projects/app
print -P 'last: %(?.ok.failed with %?)'     # last: ok
# The result looks like:
# ada@laptop ~/projects/app (main) %                     12:41
takeaways: %n %m %~ %# %? are the core prompt escapes
%F{color}...%f for colour, %(?.ok.fail) for a success-or-failure choice
PROMPT_SUBST plus single quotes for values that change, vcs_info for git
pitfalls: Writing PROMPT in double quotes with ${...}, so the value is frozen when .zshrc runs.

quiz.q: What does %(?.✔.✘) show after a failing command?
quiz.explain: %(?.a.b) shows a when the last exit status was 0 and b otherwise.

quiz.q: Why is the prompt written in single quotes with PROMPT_SUBST set?
options: So ${...} is expanded each time the prompt is drawn
Double quotes are invalid in PROMPT
quiz.explain: Single quotes keep ${...} unexpanded in the variable; PROMPT_SUBST fills it in each time the prompt is drawn.

concepts.name: Plugins, frameworks and aliases
concepts.summary: Add suggestions and colour highlighting as you type, choose between a framework and plain sourcing, and use global and suffix aliases.
concepts.why: Plugins give you suggestions and colouring as you type, but each one makes the shell slower to start.
concepts.body:
A zsh plugin is just a script you load with `source` from `.zshrc`, sometimes also adding a directory to `fpath` for its completions. Two are nearly universal:

- **zsh-autosuggestions**: shows a grey suggestion from your history as you type; Right arrow or End accepts it.
- **zsh-syntax-highlighting**: colours what you type as you type it, red for unknown commands. Load it **last**, after other plugins and keyboard shortcuts.

You can manage plugins three ways: download each with git (`git clone` copies a project from GitHub) and source it yourself; use a small plugin manager (antidote, zinit, zap); or use a **framework**, a big ready-made bundle of settings, plugins and prompt themes. **Oh My Zsh** is the best-known framework: it has hundreds of plugins (`plugins=(git docker kubectl)`) and themes. It's convenient but loads a lot; measure with `time zsh -i -c exit` and keep the list short.

Beyond normal aliases, zsh has two extra kinds:

- **global aliases** (`alias -g G='| grep -i'`) are replaced anywhere on the line, not only as the first word,
- **suffix aliases** (`alias -s md=less`) open a file when you type just its name: `README.md` runs `less README.md`.

Use global aliases sparingly: they're replaced even inside arguments where you didn't expect them. `alias` with no arguments lists everything currently defined, which helps when a framework surprises you.
concepts.code:
# Manual setup (no framework): clone once, then source in ~/.zshrc
git clone https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-autosuggestions ~/.zsh/zsh-autosuggestions
git clone https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting ~/.zsh/zsh-syntax-highlighting
# ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zsh/zsh-autosuggestions/zsh-autosuggestions.zsh
alias gs='git status'          # normal alias: command position only
alias -g G='| grep -i'         # global alias: anywhere in the line
alias -s md=less               # suffix alias: README.md -> less README.md
source ~/.zsh/zsh-syntax-highlighting/zsh-syntax-highlighting.zsh   # last
# At the prompt:
ps aux G zsh                   # runs: ps aux | grep -i zsh
time zsh -i -c exit            # how long your config takes to load
# With Oh My Zsh instead, in ~/.zshrc:  plugins=(git docker kubectl)
takeaways: Plugins are scripts you source; load zsh-syntax-highlighting last
alias -g works anywhere on the line, alias -s opens files by their name's ending
Measure startup time and keep plugins few
pitfalls: Loading dozens of Oh My Zsh plugins and then living with a one-second shell startup.

quiz.q: After `alias -g L='| less'`, what does `cat log.txt L` run?
quiz.explain: Global aliases are replaced anywhere on the line, not only in the first word.

quiz.q: Why should zsh-syntax-highlighting be sourced last?
options: It must see every key binding and editing action defined before it
It must run after compinit only
quiz.explain: It hooks into the line editor's actions, so ones defined after it wouldn't be highlighted.

concepts.name: Scripting differences from bash
concepts.summary: No word splitting, arrays counted from 1, typeset -A, the last pipe stage runs in the current shell, and `emulate` for compatibility.
concepts.why: Pasting bash snippets into zsh (or the reverse) breaks in subtle ways unless you know these differences.
concepts.body:
Zsh scripts look like bash scripts, but several defaults differ:

- **No word splitting of unquoted variables.** With `v="a b"`, `$v` stays one word. Use `${=v}` to split it on purpose, or `setopt SH_WORD_SPLIT`. Pattern characters inside a variable's value aren't expanded either, unless you write `${~v}`.
- **Arrays are counted from 1**: `$arr[1]` is the first element, `$arr[-1]` the last, `$#arr` the length, `$arr[2,3]` a slice. `$arr` alone gives all elements, and empty elements are dropped unless you use `"${arr[@]}"`.
- **Associative arrays**: `typeset -A m`; `${(k)m}` lists the keys, `${(v)m}` the values.
- `read -A` (not `-a`) reads words into an array.
- The **last part of a pipeline runs in the current shell**, so `cmd | read v` sets `v`. (Bash runs it in a separate copy of the shell, so the variable is lost.)
- A pattern that matches nothing is an error (`NOMATCH`); use `(N)`.

Prefer `print` over `echo` (`print -r --` prints text exactly as is, `print -l` one argument per line); like zsh's `echo`, plain `print` interprets backslash codes such as `\n`.

For code that must follow the rules of sh or ksh (older shells), `emulate -L sh` inside a **function** (a named group of commands, `name() { ...; }`) switches to those rules for that function only; `-L` keeps option changes inside it. The other way round, shared code meant to work under anyone's settings starts its functions with `emulate -L zsh`, to get zsh's default options.
concepts.code:
words="one two three"
for w in $words; do print -- "<$w>"; done              # <one two three>
for w in ${=words}; do print -n -- "<$w>"; done; print # <one><two><three>
arr=(alpha beta gamma)
print $arr[1] $arr[-1] $#arr          # alpha gamma 3   (1-based)
print $arr[2,3]                       # beta gamma
typeset -A port=(http 80 https 443)
print $port[https]                    # 443
print ${(k)port}                      # https http  (order not guaranteed)
echo hi | read v; print "v=$v"        # v=hi   (in bash: v=)
read -A parts <<< "x y z"; print $#parts   # 3
f() { emulate -L sh; s="a b"; set -- $s; print $#; }
f                                     # 2   (sh rules: word splitting on)
print -l -- *.nomatch(N) done         # done
takeaways: Unquoted $var is not split in zsh; ${=var} splits explicitly
Arrays start at 1; $#arr is the length
`emulate -L sh` or `emulate -L zsh` sets predictable rules inside a function
pitfalls: Porting a bash loop over `$list` and seeing it run only once, because zsh doesn't split the variable.

quiz.q: In zsh, with arr=(a b c), what is $arr[1]?
quiz.explain: Zsh arrays are counted from 1 (unless the KSH_ARRAYS option is set).

quiz.q: In zsh, `v="x y"; for i in $v; do print $i; done` prints how many lines?
quiz.explain: Zsh doesn't split unquoted variables into words by default, so the loop runs once.

concepts.name: Qualifiers, modifiers and extended globs
concepts.summary: Filter files by size, age and owner, transform paths with :t :h :r :e and use ^ and ~ with EXTENDED_GLOB.
concepts.why: These replace find, basename and dirname in one-liners, and work on variables too.
concepts.body:
Glob qualifiers combine freely inside one pair of parentheses. Sizes are counted in **bytes** (one byte holds about one letter of text): a **kilobyte** (KB) is about a thousand bytes, a **megabyte** (MB) about a million.

- **size** `L`: `(Lk+100)` larger than 100 KB, `(Lm-1)` smaller than 1 MB,
- **time** `m` (modified), `a` (accessed), `c` (changed): `(mh-1)` within the last hour, `(md+30)` more than 30 days ago,
- **owner**: `(U)` owned by you, `(u:root:)` by root; `(D)` also includes **hidden files**, whose names start with a dot,
- **sorting** with `o` (smallest first) or `O` (largest first) followed by `n` name, `L` size, `m` time changed; then a range like `[1,5]`,
- `^` reverses the next qualifier, `,` means OR between groups, and `(e:'expr':)` or `(+func)` run any test you write.

**Modifiers** change each match, and work on variables too: `:t` tail (the file name alone), `:h` head (the directory part), `:r` root (drop the ending, like `.csv`), `:e` just the ending, `:a` the path starting from `/`, `:u` and `:l` upper or lower case. `$f:t` or `${f:r}` work on any variable.

With `setopt EXTENDED_GLOB` you get extra pattern symbols: `^*.log` everything not matching, `pat~exclude` match, then leave some out, `#` and `##` for repetition, and `(#i)` to ignore upper and lower case.

Zsh also has short loop forms (`for f in *.txt; mv ...` without do/done), handy at the prompt; use the full form in scripts. To rename many files, the bundled `zmv` command (load it with `autoload -Uz zmv`) is safer than a loop.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"              # a fresh temporary directory
mkdir logs && print x > a.txt && head -c 200000 /dev/zero > big.bin
touch -d '40 days ago' logs/old.log && touch logs/new.log
print -l **/*(.Lk+100)          # big.bin         (larger than 100 KB)
print -l **/*.log(.md+30)       # logs/old.log    (changed > 30 days ago)
print -l *(.oL)                 # a.txt big.bin   (by size, smallest first)
f=/srv/app/report.final.csv
print $f:t $f:h                 # report.final.csv /srv/app
print $f:r $f:e                 # /srv/app/report.final csv
print -l logs/*(.:t:r)          # new old   (modifiers inside qualifiers)
setopt EXTENDED_GLOB
print -l *~*.bin                # a.txt logs    (~ leaves out)
print -l **/^*.log(.)           # a.txt big.bin (^ = not matching)
for f in *.txt; mv -- $f $f:r.md      # short loop form: rename .txt -> .md
print -l *(.)                   # a.md big.bin
takeaways: L size, m/a/c time, U/u owner, o/O sort, [n,m] range
:t :h :r :e modifiers work on matches and on variables
EXTENDED_GLOB adds ^ (not) and ~ (leave out)
pitfalls: Forgetting the (.) qualifier, so directories are included in a destructive command.

quiz.q: Which glob lists regular files larger than 1 MB, recursively?
quiz.explain: (.) keeps ordinary files only and Lm+1 means larger than 1 MB; mh is a time qualifier.

quiz.q: With f=photos/cat.jpeg, what does $f:r give?
quiz.explain: :r removes the ending but keeps the directory part; :t:r would give cat.

concepts.name: The line editor (ZLE) and custom widgets
concepts.summary: Configure key bindings with bindkey, use prefix history search and write your own ZLE widgets.
concepts.why: ZLE is what makes zsh's line editing programmable: any editing action can be put on any key.
concepts.body:
Everything you type at the prompt goes through **ZLE**, the Zsh Line Editor. Every action, from moving the cursor to searching history, is a **widget**, and **keymaps** connect key presses to widgets.

- `bindkey -e` selects emacs-style keys (Ctrl-A start of line, Ctrl-E end; the default unless your `EDITOR` variable mentions vi); `bindkey -v` selects vi mode, with the vi editor's keys.
- `bindkey` alone lists all bindings; `bindkey '^R'` shows one. `zle -al` lists all widgets.
- Press Ctrl-V and then a key to see the characters it sends, such as `^[[A` for Up in most terminals.

Useful bundled widgets: `up-line-or-beginning-search` makes Up search history for lines starting with what you've already typed; `edit-command-line` opens the current line in `$EDITOR`. Bundled widgets must be loaded with `autoload -Uz name` and registered with `zle -N name` before you bind them.

A **custom widget** is a shell **function** (a named group of commands, `name() { ...; }`) registered with `zle -N`. Inside it you can read and change special variables: `BUFFER` (the whole line), `LBUFFER` and `RBUFFER` (the text left and right of the cursor) and `CURSOR` (its position). `zle -M "text"` shows a message under the prompt, and `zle accept-line` runs the line. Key bindings and widgets belong in `.zshrc`, before plugins like zsh-syntax-highlighting that wrap existing widgets.
concepts.code:
bindkey -e                                  # emacs keys (-v for vi mode)
autoload -Uz up-line-or-beginning-search down-line-or-beginning-search
zle -N up-line-or-beginning-search
zle -N down-line-or-beginning-search
bindkey '^[[A' up-line-or-beginning-search  # Up: history matching the typed prefix
bindkey '^[[B' down-line-or-beginning-search
autoload -Uz edit-command-line && zle -N edit-command-line
bindkey '^X^E' edit-command-line            # edit the line in $EDITOR
# A custom widget: Alt-s puts sudo in front of the current line
prepend-sudo() {
  [[ $BUFFER == sudo\ * ]] || BUFFER="sudo $BUFFER"
  CURSOR=$#BUFFER                           # cursor to the end
  zle -M "sudo added"
}
zle -N prepend-sudo
bindkey '^[s' prepend-sudo
bindkey '^R'                                # "^R" history-incremental-search-backward
takeaways: Widgets are actions; bindkey connects keys to them
Custom widget = function + zle -N + bindkey
`BUFFER`, `LBUFFER`, `RBUFFER` and `CURSOR` give you the line being typed
pitfalls: Binding a bundled widget like edit-command-line without `autoload` and `zle -N`, which gives 'No such widget'.

quiz.q: What are the three steps to bind your own function `myw` to Ctrl-G?
options: define myw; zle -N myw; bindkey '^G' myw
quiz.explain: The function must be registered as a widget with zle -N before it can be bound.

quiz.q: Inside a widget, which variable holds the text to the left of the cursor?
quiz.explain: LBUFFER is everything before the cursor, RBUFFER everything after.

concepts.name: Parameter expansion flags
concepts.summary: Split, join, sort, deduplicate, change case and search arrays with ${(flags)name} and subscript flags.
concepts.why: Flags let zsh do in one expansion what bash needs loops or external tools for.
concepts.body:
Zsh puts **flags** in parentheses right after the opening brace: `${(flags)name}`. Several can be combined, and expansions can be nested, with the inner result feeding the outer one.

- **Split and join**: `(s:,:)` splits at a given string, `(f)` splits into lines (the usual way to turn a command's output into an array), `(j:,:)` joins with a separator, `(F)` joins into lines.
- **Case**: `(U)` upper, `(L)` lower, `(C)` capitalise words.
- **Order and uniqueness**: `(o)` sort ascending, `(O)` descending, `(n)` sort by number, `(u)` unique.
- **Associative arrays**: `(k)` keys, `(v)` values, `(kv)` pairs.
- **Quoting**: `(q)` quotes the value so it can safely be reused as shell input, `(Q)` removes one level of quoting.
- **Indirection**: `(P)` treats the value as the name of another variable and gives that variable's value.
- `(@)` keeps array elements separate inside double quotes, like `"${arr[@]}"`.

**Subscript flags** search arrays: `$arr[(i)value]` gives the position of the first match (one past the end if there is none), `$arr[(r)pattern]` the first matching element, `(I)` and `(R)` search from the end.

**Nesting** saves temporary variables: `${${f:t}%%.*}` takes the file name, then strips every ending. `${:-text}` makes a value out of fixed text, handy as the innermost expansion. Splitting with `(s)` drops empty pieces unless the expansion is quoted with `(@)`.
concepts.code:
csv="b,a,c,a"
parts=(${(s:,:)csv})
print $#parts                       # 4
print ${(j:-:)parts}                # b-a-c-a
print ${(uo)parts}                  # a b c   (unique, sorted)
print ${(U)csv}                     # B,A,C,A
lines=(${(f)"$(printf 'x 1\ny 2\n')"})
print $#lines                       # 2   (split into lines)
fruits=(apple banana cherry)
print $fruits[(i)banana]            # 2   (position of the element)
print $fruits[(i)kiwi]              # 4   (not found: length + 1)
print $fruits[(r)c*]                # cherry
ref=fruits
print ${(P)ref}                     # apple banana cherry  (indirection)
f=/a/b/archive.tar.gz
print ${${f:t}%%.*}                 # archive  (nested expansion)
s="it's here"
print -r -- ${(q)s}                 # it\'s\ here
takeaways: ${(s:x:)v} splits, ${(j:x:)arr} joins, (f) splits lines
(o) (O) (u) sort and deduplicate; (k) (v) for maps
$arr[(i)x] and $arr[(r)pat] search arrays
pitfalls: Using plain print to show (q) output: print interprets the backslashes again; use print -r.

quiz.q: What does ${(j:,:)${(s: :)${:-c a b}}} produce?
quiz.explain: The fixed text is split at spaces into (c a b) and joined with commas; no sorting flag is used.

quiz.q: With arr=(x y z), what is $arr[(i)q]?
quiz.explain: The (i) subscript gives one past the last position when nothing matches.

concepts.name: Writing completions with compsys
concepts.summary: Write a _command completion function with _arguments and _describe, register it via fpath and tune it with zstyle.
concepts.why: Completion for your own tools and scripts makes them as pleasant to use as git or docker.
concepts.body:
A completion is a function named after the command with a leading underscore, `_deploy`, stored in a file of the same name in a directory on **fpath**. The file's first line, `#compdef deploy`, tells `compinit` which commands it completes. compinit scans fpath when it builds `~/.zcompdump`, so add your directory to fpath **before** calling compinit.

Most completions are built on `_arguments`, which takes one description (a "spec") per option or argument:

- `'-v[verbose output]'` an option with a description,
- `'(-v --verbose)'{-v,--verbose}'[...]'` both spellings, each ruling out the other,
- `'--config=[config file]:file:_files'` an option that takes a value, plus the helper that completes it,
- `'1:environment:->env'` the first argument that isn't an option, handled in a `case $state` block,
- `'*:service:(api web worker)'` any further arguments, from a fixed list.

`_describe` offers values with descriptions (`'staging:test environment'`), and helpers like `_files`, `_hosts` and `_users` complete common things. For a tool whose `--help` lists its options, `compdef _gnu_generic mytool` gives decent completion for free.

Styles use the context `:completion:function:completer:command:argument:tag`, for example `zstyle ':completion:*:*:deploy:*' ...`. Press Ctrl-X then `?` to run `_complete_debug`, which writes a step-by-step record of the completion to a file. After changing completion files, remove `~/.zcompdump` and start a new shell.
concepts.code:
#compdef deploy
# file: ~/.zsh/completions/_deploy
local state
local -a envs=('staging:test environment' 'production:live site')
_arguments -s \
  '(-v --verbose)'{-v,--verbose}'[print more output]' \
  '(-t --tag)'{-t+,--tag=}'[image tag to deploy]:tag:' \
  '--config=[config file]:file:_files -g "*.(yml|yaml)"' \
  '1:environment:->env' \
  '*:service:(api web worker)'
case $state in
  env) _describe -t envs 'environment' envs ;;
esac
# In ~/.zshrc, BEFORE compinit:
#   fpath=(~/.zsh/completions $fpath)
#   autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
#   compdef _gnu_generic mytool    # free completion from mytool --help
# deploy <Tab>     ->  production -- live site / staging -- test environment
# deploy -<Tab>    ->  --config --tag --verbose -t -v
takeaways: A _cmd file with #compdef cmd on fpath, loaded by compinit
_arguments specs describe options, their values and the other arguments
->state plus case $state for custom logic; _describe for values with descriptions
pitfalls: Adding the completions directory to fpath after compinit has already run.

quiz.q: What does the first line `#compdef deploy` in a completion file do?
options: Tells compinit this function completes the deploy command
quiz.explain: compinit reads #compdef lines to know which function completes which command.

quiz.q: In an _arguments spec, what does '*:file:_files' describe?
options: Any number of further arguments completed as files
quiz.explain: A leading * means the spec applies to all remaining arguments that aren't options.

concepts.name: Autoloaded functions and startup speed
concepts.summary: Organise functions with fpath and autoload, measure startup with zprof, and speed it up with caching and loading tools on first use.
concepts.why: A shell that opens instantly is the result of knowing where your startup time goes.
concepts.body:
**Autoloading** keeps `.zshrc` small. Put each function in its own file named after it, in a directory on `fpath`, and declare it with `autoload -Uz name`. The file holds only the function's body, and nothing is read until the first call. `-U` stops aliases from being replaced while it loads (so your aliases can't break it) and `-z` selects zsh-style loading. Most of zsh's bundled features (compinit, vcs_info, zmv) are autoloaded functions.

`typeset -U path` keeps the `path` array, which is **tied** to `PATH` (change one and the other follows), free of duplicates; edit it like any array: `path=(dir $path)`. The same works for `fpath`.

To find what makes startup slow, put `zmodload zsh/zprof` at the very top of `.zshrc` and `zprof` at the bottom; it prints which functions took the most time. `time zsh -i -c exit` measures the total. The usual suspects:

- `compinit` checking and rebuilding its cache file every time: call `compinit -C` when the file is recent,
- setup scripts of tools that switch between language versions (nvm for Node.js, pyenv or conda for Python): use **lazy loading**, a small stand-in function that loads the real tool and replaces itself the first time you use it,
- frameworks loading many plugins, and commands like `brew --prefix` run at every start.

`zcompile` turns scripts and function directories into `.zwc` files, a pre-digested form called wordcode that loads faster; zsh uses them automatically when they're newer than the original.
concepts.code:
# ~/.zshrc, first line:
zmodload zsh/zprof                    # start measuring
typeset -U path fpath                 # no duplicate entries
path=(~/.local/bin $path)             # tied to $PATH
fpath=(~/.zsh/functions $fpath)
autoload -Uz mkcd                     # body lives in ~/.zsh/functions/mkcd:
#   mkdir -p -- "$1" && cd -- "$1"
nvm() { unfunction nvm; source ~/.nvm/nvm.sh; nvm "$@"; }   # load on first use
autoload -Uz compinit
setopt EXTENDED_GLOB
if [[ -n ~/.zcompdump(#qN.mh+24) ]]; then
  compinit                            # cache older than 24 h: full check
else
  compinit -C                         # recent cache: skip the check
fi
zcompile ~/.zshrc                     # writes ~/.zshrc.zwc
# last line:
zprof | head -n 15                    # functions sorted by time spent
takeaways: autoload -Uz name loads the file name from fpath on first call
zmodload zsh/zprof + zprof finds slow startup code
Lazy-load heavy tools and use compinit -C with a recent cache
pitfalls: Running `eval "$(slow-tool init)"` for several tools at every start instead of loading them on first use.

quiz.q: What does `autoload -Uz mkcd` do immediately?
options: Reads and parses the mkcd file
Marks mkcd to be loaded from fpath on first use
quiz.explain: autoload only registers the name; the file is read when the function is first called.

quiz.q: How do you see which parts of .zshrc are slow?
options: zmodload zsh/zprof at the top, zprof at the bottom
quiz.explain: zprof reports the time spent in each function since the zprof module was loaded.
